# The Weight of Empty Rooms

There is something about a room that has just been emptied of its furniture that feels like a held breath. The floors show ghostly rectangles where the couch sat for fourteen years. Pale spots where a bookcase stood, shielding the wall from years of sunlight. The scuff marks near the doorway tell a story of thousands of passages — someone going out to work, someone coming home tired, someone pacing during a phone call they didn't want to have.

I don't know why I started there. Empty rooms. Maybe because I spend so much time building things that don't exist — worlds, characters, arguments, systems of thought — and the blank page before I begin is something like that stripped-down room. Full of potential. Full of echoes. Waiting for the furniture to be moved back in.

Language is a strange instrument. We use it so casually, so carelessly, tossing words around like they cost nothing. But words do cost something. Every sentence committed to writing is a small act of architecture. You choose this word and not that one, and the shape of what you've built changes. Not just the shape — the weight of it. The color. *Melancholy* is not the same as *sadness*. *Home* is not the same as *house*. A child knows this instinctively. An adult has to relearn it, usually through suffering.

I think about time more than I probably should. Not the clock kind — not deadlines and appointments and the tyranny of the calendar. I mean the felt kind. The way a Tuesday afternoon in November can feel like it lasts a week while an entire year dissolves into a single blurry impression of warmth and motion. Childhood is like that. I can remember being seven with startling clarity — the exact shade of the sky through the kitchen window, the sound of gravel under my bike tires, the heavy book about dinosaurs that I carried everywhere even though I couldn't yet read most of it. But try to recall last Thursday in detail and it's gone. Wiped. A blank wall with a rectangle where the couch used to be.

There is a theory in physics — the block universe — which says that all moments in time exist simultaneously, the way all points in space exist simultaneously. Past, present, and future are all just coordinates. The dinosaurs are still stomping around out there. Your grandmother is still alive. You are still a child, learning to ride that bike on the gravel driveway. If this is true, then nothing is ever lost. Everything is just *elsewhere*. I find this oddly comforting and deeply terrifying at the same time, the way most true things are.

The human brain weighs about three pounds. Inside those three pounds: every song you've ever loved, every face that made your stomach flip, every single thing you've ever smelled. The specific smell of rain on hot asphalt. The smell of the detergent your mother used in 1993. The smell of your own skin when you were too young to know you had skin. Three pounds. It all fits in there. And when you die, those three pounds become, justifiably, just three pounds of warm tissue that rapidly stops being warm. Where does the music go? Where does the gravel driveway go?

I don't know. And I don't think anyone does, not really, though many pretend otherwise.

What I do know is that writing — the act of putting these particular words in this particular order — is the closest I come to planting a flag in the sand before the tide comes in. It won't hold. None of it holds. But for this moment, in this room that is both empty and full, I have said *this happened* and *I felt that* and *the light looked like this*. And someone, maybe, on the other side of time or language or loneliness, will read it and think: *yes, me too*.

That is enough. It has to be.

Because the other option is silence, and silence, though vast and honest and important in its own right, doesn't have room for *melancholy* versus *sadness*. It doesn't have the word *home*. It cannot build anything at all.

So I write. Three-pound brain, borrowed words, borrowed time. A room filling slowly with furniture that I know I will have to carry out again someday.

But not yet. Not yet.

---

*Word count: ~730*
